claims.source: Thus, all the molecular species (i.e., Ds and DsP and Ft and FtP) contribute to the final population of bound Ft and Ds at cell junctions.
claims.evidence: Inferred from modest effects of blocking individual phosphorylation events

claims.claim: The ability of the gradient of phosphorylated Dachsous to oppose the gradient of phosphorylated Fat is reduced due to the stronger effect of Four-jointed on Fat
claims.source: A simple prediction of this observation, confirmed by our computational model, is that the ability of the gradient of phosphorylated Ds to oppose the gradient of phosphorylated Ft is reduced, and therefore a gradient of Ft–Ds binding is expected to be observed across the tissue (Figures 5A and 6A).
claims.evidence: Predicted by computational model and confirmed experimentally

claims.claim: The computational model results in relatively modest cellular asymmetries of Fat and Dachsous distributions (around 10% of the total cellular levels)
claims.source: We note that our computational simulations result in relatively modest cellular asymmetries of Ft and Ds distributions (around 10% of the total cellular levels), whereas in vivo, observed Ds asymmetry can be as high as twofold (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental observations from cited studies

claims.claim: In vivo, observed Dachsous asymmetry can be as high as twofold
claims.source: We note that our computational simulations result in relatively modest cellular asymmetries of Ft and Ds distributions (around 10% of the total cellular levels), whereas in vivo, observed Ds asymmetry can be as high as twofold (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous experimental studies

claims.claim: The computational model does not capture the full complexity of a three-dimensional cell environment and changes that occur in protein production and degradation and other cell properties over time
claims.source: However, our model is only intended to make simple predictions regarding the effects of binding and redistribution of Ft and Ds molecules in a simple one-dimensional system and does not capture the full complexity of a three-dimensional cell environment and changes that occur in protein production and degradation and other cell properties over time.
claims.evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the modeling approach

claims.claim: Relatively weak asymmetries generated by expression gradients might be amplified by feedback mechanisms
claims.source: Furthermore, it is generally believed that relatively weak asymmetries generated by expression gradients might subsequently be amplified by feedback mechanisms (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012), and some molecular mechanisms that might contribute to amplification have recently been identified (Bosch et al., 2014; Rodrigues-Campos and Thompson, 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claims.claim: The majority of stable Fat–Dachsous at junctions is concentrated in bright regions referred to as puncta
claims.source: With regard to possible amplification mechanisms, an intriguing observation is that the majority of stable Ft–Ds at junctions is concentrated in bright regions which we refer to as 'puncta'.
claims.evidence: Observed from imaging and FRAP experiments

claims.claim: Mobile junctional populations of Fat and Dachsous show reduced mobility within puncta regions
claims.source: Furthermore, even mobile junctional populations of Ft and Ds show reduced mobility within these brighter regions.
claims.evidence: Observed from FRAP rate analysis

claims.claim: There may be cis-interactions between Fat and Dachsous molecules in cell junctions
claims.source: This might suggest that in addition to trans-interactions between Ft and Ds in neighbouring cells, there may also be cis-interactions between Ft and Ds molecules in cell junctions, a view supported by previous experimental reports (Matakatsu and Blair, 2006; Sopko et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous studies

claims.claim: A clustering mechanism involving cis-interactions could provide the molecular basis of a positive feedback interaction
claims.source: Such a clustering mechanism could provide the molecular basis of a positive feedback interaction.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation of puncta formation

claims.claim: Fat–Dachsous puncta do not co-localise with core planar polarity protein puncta at junctions
claims.source: Previous observations have suggested that Ft–Ds puncta do not co-localise with 'core' planar polarity protein puncta at junctions (Ma et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claims.claim: Fat-Dachsous puncta could correspond to specialised membrane domains that favour binding
claims.source: We are unsure as to the reasons for these distinct puncta populations, they could correspond to specialised membrane domains that favour binding or they could be random regions of protein clustering driven by cis-dimerisation or cytoskeleton tethering.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation of puncta nature

claims.claim: Fat-Dachsous puncta could be random regions of protein clustering driven by cis-dimerisation or cytoskeleton tethering
claims.source: We are unsure as to the reasons for these distinct puncta populations, they could correspond to specialised membrane domains that favour binding or they could be random regions of protein clustering driven by cis-dimerisation or cytoskeleton tethering.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation of puncta nature

claims.claim: Modification of analogous serine residues in cadherin repeats of Fat and Dachsous by Four-jointed phosphorylation leads to opposite effects on their binding activity
claims.source: A final conundrum is the observation, first made in vitro, which we have now confirmed in vivo, that modification of analogous serine residues in cadherin repeats of Ft and Ds by Fj phosphorylation leads to opposite effects on their binding activity.
claims.evidence: Confirmed by in vivo experiments building on previous in vitro observations

claims.claim: Phosphorylation events may lead to changes in the intramolecular conformation of the extracellular regions of Fat and Dachsous
claims.source: A possible working hypothesis is that phosphorylation events lead to changes in the intramolecular conformation of the extracellular regions of Ft and Ds, by analogy to the way in which phosphorylation frequently acts to cause other classes of molecules to enter 'open' or 'closed' conformations (Xu and Carpenter, 1999; Potter et al., 2005; Bertocchi et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Speculative hypothesis supported by citations to analogous mechanisms

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of each molecule (Fat and Dachsous) may cause it to enter an open conformation, with open Fat binding most favourably to Dachsous and closed Dachsous binding most favourably to Fat
claims.source: A possible scenario is that phosphorylation of each molecule causes it to enter an 'open' conformation, and that 'open' Ft binds most favourably to Ds, but 'closed' Ds binds most favourably to Ft (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Speculative model illustrated in Figure 6B

claims.claim: Mammalian Fat4 and Dachsous1 have multiple hairpin-like bends in their C-terminal regions caused by the loss of calcium binding linkers
claims.source: A recent publication analysing the configuration of mammalian Ft4 and Ds1 revealed multiple hairpin-like bends in their C-terminal regions caused by the loss of calcium binding linkers (Tsukasaki et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to recent structural study

claims.claim: Four-jointed phosphorylation may result in conformational changes between cadherin repeat domains near calcium binding sites resulting in the regulation of binding strength
claims.source: It is possible that Fj phosphorylation results in conformational changes between cadherin repeat domains near to these calcium binding sites resulting in the regulation of binding strength, as suggested previously for E-cadherin (Petrova et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation to analogous mechanism in E-cadherin

claims.claim: A hierarchy of binding affinities was used in the computational model, with phosphorylated Fat and unphosphorylated Dachsous producing the strongest partnership, and unphosphorylated Fat and phosphorylated Dachsous producing the weakest partnership
claims.source: A hierarchy of binding affinities was used, based on the in vitro experiments (Brittle et al., 2010; Simon et al., 2010), with phosphorylated Ft (FtP) and unphosphorylated Ds (Ds) producing the strongest partnership, and unphosphorylated Ft (Ft) and phosphorylated Ds (DsP) producing the weakest partnership (see 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: Based on in vitro experimental results from cited studies

claims.claim: Ft and Ds are allowed to redistribute in the computational model in accordance with experimental observations of protein mobility
claims.source: We also allowed redistribution of Ft and Ds to occur in the model, in accordance with our experimental observations of protein mobility (see Figure 2C,D,L).
claims.evidence: Model parameter based on experimental FRAP data

claims.claim: In the computational model, Four-jointed is allowed to phosphorylate either Fat or Dachsous in proportion to its concentration
claims.source: In the model, Fj is allowed to phosphorylate either Ft or Ds in proportion to its concentration, and Ft and Ds are then permitted to freely bind at cell edges until they reach equilibrium (see Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Description of model design

claims.claim: In the computational model, Fat and Dachsous are permitted to freely bind at cell edges until they reach equilibrium
claims.source: In the model, Fj is allowed to phosphorylate either Ft or Ds in proportion to its concentration, and Ft and Ds are then permitted to freely bind at cell edges until they reach equilibrium (see Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Description of model design

claims.claim: The computational model reflects a one-dimensional line of cells each with two compartments to simulate Fat–Dachsous binding between cells according to a Four-jointed gradient
claims.source: As an aid to understand the possible consequences for the generation of cellular asymmetry of Fj acting on either Ft or Ds or both, we generated a computational model reflecting a one-dimensional line of cells each with two compartments, to simulate Ft–Ds binding between cells according to a Fj gradient (see 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: Description of model design

claims.claim: A Four-jointed gradient can lead to cellular asymmetry of Fat–Dachsous if Fj acts on either Ft or Ds or both
claims.source: Using this we show that a Fj gradient can lead to cellular asymmetry of Ft–Ds if Fj acts on either Ft or Ds or both.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by computational modeling

claims.claim: The predictions of the current model differ from a previous study which suggested that Four-jointed acting only on Fat would not result in a cellular asymmetry of activity
claims.source: Our predictions differ from those of a previous study (Simon et al., 2010) which suggested that Fj acting only on Ft would not result in a cellular asymmetry of activity: the origin of this difference is that in our model (in accordance with our experimental observations) the Ft and Ds populations are mobile and able to redistribute to the most favourable cell edge.
claims.evidence: Comparison with previous modeling study, explained by different model assumptions

claims.claim: In the current model, the Fat and Dachsous populations are mobile and able to redistribute to the most favourable cell edge
claims.source: Our predictions differ from those of a previous study (Simon et al., 2010) which suggested that Fj acting only on Ft would not result in a cellular asymmetry of activity: the origin of this difference is that in our model (in accordance with our experimental observations) the Ft and Ds populations are mobile and able to redistribute to the most favourable cell edge.
claims.evidence: Model design based on experimental observations

claims.claim: Only in the situation that Four-jointed acts on both Fat and Dachsous is the amount of Fat–Dachsous dimers bound at the junctions approximately the same across the entire axis of the Four-jointed gradient
claims.source: However, in agreement with the same study, our model does predict that only in the situation that Fj acts on both Ft and Ds is the amount of Ft–Ds dimers bound at the junctions approximately the same across the entire axis of the Fj gradient.
claims.evidence: Predicted by computational model, in agreement with previous study

results.result: A gradient of 2.5–3.5% Four-jointed expression between adjacent cells was measured along the proximo-distal axis in Drosophila larval wing discs.
results.evaluation: Claim C14 is supported by direct measurements from wing disc images with appropriate background correction using fj null clones (Figure 1B, C). The methodology is sound and the quantification is clearly described.

results.result: Computational modeling predicts that a Four-jointed gradient can generate cellular asymmetry of Fat-Dachsous binding whether Fj acts on Ft only, Ds only, or both, with the strongest asymmetry (7.9%) and minimal tissue gradient when Fj acts on both proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 present computational modeling predictions that are internally consistent and based on reasonable assumptions (C108-C109). The model is clearly described with specific quantitative predictions for different scenarios. However, the model is acknowledged to be simplified (C90) and produces more modest asymmetries (~10%) than observed in vivo (twofold, C89).

results.result: EGFP-tagged versions of Fat and Dachsous localize similarly to wild-type proteins and are expressed at comparable levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 are supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification (Figure 2A, B). The validation of tagged proteins is essential for subsequent FRAP experiments and appears adequately demonstrated.

results.result: Fat-EGFP and Dachsous-EGFP exhibit large stable fractions concentrated in bright puncta regions at cell junctions, with significantly more stable protein in puncta compared to non-puncta regions (p = 0.0001 for both).
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25 and C92 are supported by FRAP experiments with clear statistical significance (Figure 2C, D). The methodology is well-described and the distinction between puncta and non-puncta is quantitatively validated. The stable fraction analysis appropriately accounts for pre-bleach intensity levels.

results.result: Fat puncta persist over time during antibody internalization assays while total apical Fat levels decrease significantly, and internalized Fat co-localizes with early endosome marker Hrs.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by time-course imaging with statistical analysis (p = 0.01 at 10 min, p = 0.001 at 20 min) and co-localization data (Figure 2E, F). This provides independent validation of stable and unstable protein populations observed in FRAP experiments.

results.result: Fat and Dachsous require each other for junctional stability, as removal of either binding partner results in loss of puncta, nearly complete fluorescence recovery after bleaching, and increased protein mobility.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32, C35-C36, and C44-C45 are well-supported by FRAP experiments in mutant backgrounds (Figure 2G-J). The loss of stability and puncta in the absence of binding partners provides strong evidence for heterophilic binding. The conclusion is logically sound and directly supported by the data.

results.result: There is almost twice as much Fat-EGFP as Dachsous-EGFP in puncta regions (p = 0.01).
results.evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by quantitative comparison at identical confocal settings (Figure 2K). However, the comparison is limited by different sample sizes (n=4 wings for Ft vs n=2 wings for Ds), which weakens the statistical power. The finding is used to explain differential mobility patterns (C43).

results.result: Mobile fractions of Fat-EGFP and Dachsous-EGFP exhibit slower recovery in puncta compared to non-puncta, with Ds showing reduced mobility in the presence of Ft, suggesting both immobile and mobile bound populations exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C37-C38, and C41-C43 are supported by rate analysis from FRAP data (Table 1, Figure 2L). The interpretation that slower mobility indicates binding is reasonable. However, C43 involves inference about excess Ft based on C33, which has limited sample size. The overall conclusion about mobile bound populations is well-reasoned.

results.result: The reduced mobility of Fat-Dachsous heterodimers in puncta may indicate cis-dimerization mechanisms or cytoskeletal interactions that promote clustering.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 and C94-C95, C97-C98 are explicitly speculative interpretations of the puncta observations. While supported by citations to analogous mechanisms (C40, C94), these remain hypotheses without direct experimental validation in this study. The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty (C97-C98).

results.result: Removal of Four-jointed results in reduced stability of both Fat-EGFP and Dachsous-EGFP at junctions, with the net effect indicating that Fj's effect on Fat is dominant to its effect on Dachsous.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 are supported by FRAP experiments in fj mutant backgrounds with statistical significance (p = 0.004 for Ds, p = 0.04 for Ft) (Figure 3). The inference that Fj's effect on Ft is dominant (C50) is logical given the net loss of stability rather than gain. This is a key finding that distinguishes in vivo effects from in vitro predictions.

results.result: Mutating Dachsous phosphorylation sites to prevent Fj phosphorylation significantly increases stable protein (p = 0.0004), but this increase is lost when Fj is also removed, confirming Fj acts on Ds but with effects dependent on Ft phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 and C59-C60 are supported by FRAP experiments with Ds phosphomutants (Figure 4A, B, E). The experimental design appropriately isolates the effect of Ds phosphorylation by maintaining Fj expression. The loss of the phosphomutant advantage when Fj is removed (C53) provides strong evidence for the dominant effect of Ft phosphorylation.

results.result: Fat phosphomutant shows decreased stable fraction and reduced stable amount (p = 0.006), and removal of Fj from this background does not significantly change stability, confirming the reduction is primarily due to loss of Ft phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by FRAP experiments with Ft phosphomutants (Figure 4C, D). The lack of change when Fj is removed from the Ft phosphomutant background (C56) provides strong evidence that the observed effects are specifically due to Ft phosphorylation rather than indirect effects through Ds.

results.result: Phosphomutant experiments reveal in vivo effects of Four-jointed phosphorylation on both Fat and Dachsous, confirming that phosphorylation of analogous residues leads to opposite effects on binding activity, with a dominant effect on Fat.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C61, and C99 synthesize the phosphomutant results and confirm in vivo what was previously observed in vitro. The evidence from multiple complementary experiments (C51-C57) strongly supports these conclusions. This represents a major advance in understanding the in vivo mechanism.

results.result: Revised computational modeling with Ft phosphorylation bias predicts cellular asymmetry of 4.1% and a tissue gradient of 4.7%, suggesting Ds phosphorylation is required to counter the strong graded effects of Ft phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 and C87 present revised model predictions incorporating the experimentally determined Ft bias. The model predictions are internally consistent and provide testable hypotheses. The prediction of a tissue gradient (C63) is subsequently tested experimentally (C65-C72), providing validation.

results.result: Endogenously expressed Dachsous-EGFP shows significantly increased stable amount in high Four-jointed regions (p = 0.01, 23% difference), and this difference is lost in fj mutants, confirming a gradient of Fat-Dachsous binding strength exists across the tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 and C70 are supported by FRAP experiments across the Fj gradient (Figure 5B, C). The statistical significance is adequate, and the loss of the gradient in fj mutants (C67) provides strong evidence that the observed difference is Fj-dependent. This directly validates the model prediction.

results.result: Dachsous phosphomutant shows a greater difference in stable protein between high and low Fj regions (p = 0.01, 53% difference), which is lost upon Fj removal, demonstrating that opposing gradients of Ds and Ft phosphorylation result in relatively even distribution of bound complexes across the tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 and C71-C72 are supported by FRAP experiments with Ds phosphomutants across the Fj gradient (Figure 5E, F). The larger difference in the phosphomutant (53% vs 23%) demonstrates that Ds phosphorylation normally opposes the Ft phosphorylation gradient. This is a key finding that validates the model and demonstrates the mechanism of gradient interpretation.

results.result: Four-jointed acts on Fat to promote its binding to Dachsous and on Dachsous to inhibit its binding to Fat in vivo, with a stronger effect on Fat, and opposing gradients of phosphorylation are sufficient to explain the observed pattern of Fat-Dachsous binding and planar polarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 represent the main conclusions of the paper and are supported by the comprehensive set of FRAP experiments (C46-C72), phosphomutant analyses (C51-C61), and computational modeling (C62-C64). The integration of experimental and computational approaches provides strong support for the mechanism. This is the central finding of the study.

results.result: The effects of Four-jointed on Fat-Dachsous binding are relatively modest, with blocking phosphorylation of either protein decreasing stable amounts by only about twofold, indicating all molecular species contribute to the final bound population.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are supported by observations from FRAP experiments (C51, C55). The interpretation that all species contribute (C86) is reasonable given the modest effects. This observation is important for understanding the biological mechanism and explains why the model produces more modest asymmetries than observed in vivo.

results.result: The computational model produces modest cellular asymmetries (~10%) compared to observed in vivo asymmetries (up to twofold), which is acknowledged as a limitation of the simplified one-dimensional model that does not capture feedback amplification mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 acknowledge limitations of the modeling approach. C88-C89 compare model predictions to experimental observations from cited studies. C90 explicitly acknowledges model limitations. C91 cites evidence for amplification mechanisms. This represents appropriate scientific caution and suggests directions for future work.

results.result: Mobile junctional populations of Fat and Dachsous show reduced mobility within puncta regions.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 is supported by FRAP rate analysis (Table 1, Figure 2L). This observation contributes to understanding the nature of puncta and potential clustering mechanisms.

results.result: Phosphorylation may lead to conformational changes in Fat and Dachsous, with a possible scenario where phosphorylation causes an 'open' conformation and open Fat binds most favorably to Dachsous while closed Dachsous binds most favorably to Fat.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 and C103 are explicitly speculative hypotheses (supported by citations to analogous mechanisms) to explain the opposite effects of phosphorylation on Ft and Ds binding. While reasonable, these remain untested hypotheses. The authors appropriately present these as working hypotheses requiring further structural studies.

results.result: The computational model incorporates a hierarchy of binding affinities based on in vitro experiments, allows protein redistribution based on experimental mobility observations, and permits Fat and Dachsous to freely bind until equilibrium.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 and C111 describe the computational model design and parameters. The model is based on experimental data (C104-C105) and reasonable assumptions (C106-C107). The inclusion of protein mobility (C111) distinguishes this model from previous work (C110) and is justified by experimental observations.

results.result: The current model differs from a previous study by including protein mobility, and predicts that only when Fj acts on both Ft and Ds is the amount of bound dimers approximately the same across the Fj gradient.
results.evaluation: Claims C110 and C112 compare the current model to previous work. C110 explains the difference in predictions based on inclusion of protein mobility. C112 notes agreement with previous work on one key prediction. This appropriately contextualizes the current work within the field.

results.result: Background claims about Fat-Dachsous-Four-jointed system properties, expression patterns, and prior in vitro findings establish the context for the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C13, C73-C83, C96, and C102 are background claims supported by citations to previous studies. These appropriately establish the scientific context and prior knowledge upon which the current study builds. The citations appear appropriate and accurate.
